content: I currently have a stack of PRs forming on Hahn series, so I’m starting a thread.
#6208 is needed to define multiplication, and #6226 is needed to show the product is an actual Hahn series.
These are put to work in branch#hahn_series.
I’m interested in any thoughts as to whether Laurent series should actually be defined as hahn_series Z _, or if I should just give an iso when both are done.
@Kevin Buzzard
My plan was to define Laurent series as Hahn series with coefficients in Z and to prove that that were a localisation of power series in one variable at the variable. Thanks so much for doing this!
Ok, #6237 gets up to the comm_ring structure.
Cool! You are moving fast!
How nice! You did a really nice job, I am learning a lot reading what you did.
Let me know if you have any further questions about it, it'd help the documentation.

Other than the order theory, creating a new type of series with a convolution product is a bit boilerplate, except for a few small things that can go wrong in the distributivity/associativity proofs, which go wrong differently in each different context it seems...

While @Aaron Anderson was developing the more powerful theory of Hahn Series, I've amused myself defining Laurent series (in one variable), and PR it in #6258. There are still some sorrys left concerning associativity, but the basics of it being a comm_ring (when the coefficients are) is there. I've also defined coefficients (as a function from Z\mathbb{Z}Z to the base ring). Being much less experienced then @Aaron Anderson , my code is by far less efficient and I wonder if anything of what I've done should be kept or if the approach through Hahn series makes everything obsolete. Before going further, I'd appreciate if anyone can have a look and tell me if it is worth spending more time on my approach, or not.
I think the biggest issue is that working with quotients is difficult.

Personally I think it's much easier to define Laurent series as a subtype of a type of functions like how I defined Hahn series, or if you want to use ordered pairs, make the pair representation unique, like perhaps by representing it as a pair of a coefficient function with a rank, where the rank lives in with_top Z, with the rule that the rank is the largest possible rank such that all coefficients below that rank are 0.

The benefit of your sort of pair representation is in defining the embedding of power series into Laurent series, and I'll admit I haven't gotten there yet, but I think it should still not be too bad with Hahn series
The actual Hahn series PR #6237 is now unblocked. I've started developing the valuation at branch#hahn_series2, but won't be able to get around to it again for at least a week.
An update on the Hahn series project if anyone wants it:
I'm inching closer towards being able to define the field structure. The critical step that remains is proving Higman's Lemma.

To do that, I started expanding the API on partial well-orderings, and in the process of looking into all of this, found that with partial well-orderings, we can drop the linearity assumption on the monomial group, which means that things like multivariable Laurent series should be possible. This is what #7131 is for.

I've delayed defining Laurent series until I have the field structure, so I can define the localization map as a localization map, but if anyone has any requests for Laurent series API, I'd be happy to discuss it.

@Aaron Anderson This is becoming a pretty huge project, but I'm really happy you are doing it. I don't have a pressing need for Laurent series right now. But probably in a couple of months, yes.
And it's just great to know that by that time there will be a solid API in place!
Yes this is a much overdue API. Many thanks!
Yes, this is rather more complicated than just defining Laurent series, but we should also be able to get Puiseux series for cheap, and Hahn series themselves are nice.

Resurrecting this thread years later because I have a question regarding the relationship between docs#HahnSeries and docs#MvPowerSeries
Mathematically powerseries are Hahn series. In Lean I guess we only have Mathlib.RingTheory.HahnSeries.PowerSeries.

Sorry, I ran to other things! Here is the actual question: For several months now, I thought MvPowerSeries σ R was mathematically identical to HahnSeries (σ →₀ ℕ) R. However, trying to remove the Finite σ assumption from docs#HahnSeries.toMvPowerSeries, I understood that this wasn't the case.
Did I understand this correctly by saying that X_0 + X_1 + X_2 +... is a MvPowerSeries, but not a HahnSereis?
Is it HahnSeries (Lex (σ →₀ ℕ)) R with some arbitrary well order on σ?

It's mathematically identical to (σ →₀ ℕ) → R so it's HahnSeries X R iff X = σ →₀ ℕ with a partial order imposed on X such that ∀ (s : Set X), s.IsPWO, which I guess boils down to the statement that X is well-quasi-ordered by ≤. For Lex I my instinct is that this is indeed true for a well-order on σ, because then σ →₀ ℕ is totally ordered and you won't have enough space for an infinite descending sequence, but this is only an instinct.

NB docs#Set.PartiallyWellOrderedOn seems to have some nonsense in the docstring -- a set surely isn't partially well-ordered by a relation iff any antichain is finite -- consider any well-ordered set for example.

Apologies, I disappeared again before I said what I wanted to say! The issue is that MvPowerSeries σ R contains all functions f : (σ →₀ ℕ) → R, but HahnSeries (σ →₀ ℕ) R only contains those functions f whose support is well-quasi-ordered (ie for any sequence α : ℕ → σ →₀ ℕ such that f (α n) ≠ 0 for all n, there exist m and n such that m ≤ n and α m ≤ α n). Well-quasi-ordering is equivalent to well-foundedness over linear orders (cf docs#Set.isPWO_iff_isWF), but in a general partial order well-quasi-ordering is weaker.

The crucial point is that, to define multiplication on HahnSeries M R, we need to restrict the possible supports to sets in M such that, for any two allowed supports s and t and any element a : M, there are only finitely many pairs b, c such that a = b * c.

The way HahnSeries M R achieves this is by allowing exactly the supports that are well-quasi-ordered. The way MvPowerSeries σ R achieves this is that σ →₀ ℕ is a well-founded canonical order, and therefore a = b * c has finitely many solutions in b and c full stop.

My question now is whether it is possible to extend the supports allowed in HahnSeries M R in such a way that they still respect the finiteness of solutions condition and so that all supports are allowed in the special case of M := σ →₀ ℕ
Didn't Andrew answer this? Well-order sigma and use Lex, which presumably well-orders σ →₀ ℕ (extending the partial order you know). You don't need to extend supports.
This is unsatisfactory: If the answer doesn't depend on the well-order of σ, then why do I need to introduce it in the first place?

The Hahn theory is essentially an ordered theory and applies in situations like Laurent series where it is not true that the set of solutions to x+y=z is finite for a given z, but where the ordering plays a crucial role. You are observing that there's also a theory where the indices are valued in an additive monoid with a finiteness property (number of solutions to x+y=z is finite for all z) and are attempting to then canonically order the monoid using the addition law and apply the Hahn theory. Why not just stick to the finiteness hypothesis?

... because this involves an apparent duplication of a lot of API with various name mismatches and missing declarations. I have spent the last year trying to unify various monoid algebra-like objects, and I would be sad to hear that HahnSeries and MvPowerSeries cannot be unified.

The reason that products are well-defined seem to be distinct though. One is that there are only finitely many solutions to an equation, the other is that for an order-theoretic reason there are only finitely many relevant solutions in any given situation. Doesn't the argument above show that neither situation can be reduced to the other?

There is a global reason why multiplication of power series is well-defined and it's algebraic (a finiteness result); the reason why multiplication of Hahn series is well-defined is local, it depends on the series you're mutiplying and it's order-theoretic. I guess you want some kind of common generalization rather than reducing one theory to the other?
Yes, exactly. Alternatively, we decree that X_0 + X_1 + X_2 +... isn't a multivariate power series, but this seems unsatisfactory as well
I don't think "change a standard definition so that it fits into a box which Yael wants it to fit into" is going to get much traction :-)

Sure... but have you ever seen a power series in infinitely many variables? I personally haven't, and wonder if docs#MvPowerSeries really is a "standard definition" in the generality we currently have it

Google AI's summary

Whether x1+x2+x3+…x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + \dotsx1​+x2​+x3​+… is considered a valid formal power series depends entirely on which of the two common definitions of the ring of formal power series in infinitely many variables you choose. [1, 2]
There is no single "canonical" definition for countably many variables, and the validity of such a sum depends on the construction used: [1]

  1. The "Large" Ring (Bourbaki Definition)
    In this construction, an element is defined as any formal sum of monomials where each individual monomial involves only finitely many variables. [1, 2]
    * Validity: The sum x1+x2+x3+…x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + \dotsx1​+x2​+x3​+… is valid in this ring.
    * Logic: Each term (x1,x2x_1, x_2x1​,x2​, etc.) is a valid monomial. Because there are no restrictions on the total number of terms, you can have infinitely many distinct degree-1 terms.
    * Pros/Cons: This ring is very large and "unruly." For instance, it is often not a completion of the polynomial ring in a standard topological sense. [1, 2, 3, 4]

  2. The "Small" Ring (Inverse Limit/Completion Definition)
    This version is often defined as the inverse limit of finite-variable rings: R[[x1,x2,… ]]=lim←⁡R[[x1,…,xn]]R[[x_1, x_2, \dots]] = \varprojlim R[[x_1, \dots, x_n]]R[[x1​,x2​,…]]=lim​R[[x1​,…,xn​]]. Alternatively, it is seen as the completion of the polynomial ring R[x1,x2,… ]R[x_1, x_2, \dots]R[x1​,x2​,…] with respect to the ideal generated by all variables (x1,x2,… )(x_1, x_2, \dots)(x1​,x2​,…). [1, 2, 3]
    * Validity: The sum x1+x2+x3+…x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + \dotsx1​+x2​+x3​+… is not valid in this ring.
    * Logic: In this topology, for a sum to be well-defined, the number of terms of any given degree must be finite. Since there are infinitely many variables of degree 1 (x1,x2,…x_1, x_2, \dotsx1​,x2​,…), their sum does not "converge" to an element in the completion.
    * Pros/Cons: This ring is better behaved algebraically (e.g., it is a local ring and often a Unique Factorization Domain) and feels more like a natural extension of the finite-variable case. [1, 2, 3]

Summary of Validity
* Is it a valid series? Yes, if you use the definition that allows arbitrary formal sums of monomials (the "large" ring).
* Is it a valid series? No, if you require the ring to be the standard (x1,x2,… )(x_1, x_2, \dots)(x1​,x2​,…)-adic completion of the polynomial ring (the "small" ring). [1, 2]

:check: Answer
Whether x1+x2+x3+…x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + \dotsx1​+x2​+x3​+… is a valid formal power series depends on the specific definition of the ring; it is valid in the "large" ring of arbitrary formal sums but invalid in the standard "small" ring defined as the adic completion of polynomials.

It is however not an element of the completion of the polynomial ring R[X_0,X_1,...] with respect to the ideal (X_0,X_1,...) (a ring which the AI slop incorrectly identifies with the projective limit of the finite power series rings)

If we really need these different series rings, then perhaps we should have a general definition that takes the allowed supports as a parameter (a bornology with some extra conditions?).

I have been thinking about this question a bit because I'm interested in formalizing symmetric functions for mathlib. There is a generalized monoid algebra construction which I believe captures all the examples here (e.g. Hahn series as well). I've written a short note about it: https://ajdobner.github.io/notes/generalized_monoid_algebras.pdf

It's possible that this level of generality is overkill, but using a generalized monoid algebra construction is useful for certain things. For example, in the symmetric functions case there is an action of the symmetric group on the variables, which would then lift to an action on MvPowerSeries by general principles.

Yes, finiteness of antidiagonals and closure under finite setwise sums are the key properties for support. As long as we are generalizing, do we want a notion that also includes maximal extensions of nonarchimedean valued fields? They also have a Hahn-series-like characterization.

The construction in §2 is called “algèbre large d'un monoïde” (large algebra of a monoid) in Bourbaki, Algèbre, chapter 3. The case of Hahn series is done in exercises (chap. 3, §2, exerc. 26) exactly as you do.
This is definitely something we should have.

Yes, there is also a wikipedia page on the total monoid algebra (with a reference to Bourbaki). I don't think Bourbaki goes into axiomatizing the support restriction?
It would be nice to know if there are other useful examples of this construction (other than (i) Hahn series and (ii) multivariate power series with bounded total degree). I'm not familiar with the example Scott mentioned.
